'''''Yucca glauca''''' ([[syn.]] ''Yucca angustifolia'') is a species of [[perennial]] [[evergreen]] plant, adapted to [[xeric]] (dry) growth conditions. It is also known as '''small soapweed''',<ref name=NAE/> '''soapweed yucca''', '''Spanish bayonet''',<ref>Schiemann, Donald Anthony. Wildflowers of Montana. page 140. Mountain Press Publishing Company. Missoula. 2005.</ref>   and '''Great Plains yucca'''.

''Yucca glauca'' forms colonies of rosettes. Leaves are long and narrow, up to 60 cm long but rarely more than 12 mm across. Inflorescence is up to 100 cm tall, sometimes branched sometimes not. Flowers are pendent (drooping, hanging downward), white to very pale green. Fruit is a dry capsule with shiny black seeds.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242102064 Flora of North America v 26 p 437, ''Yucca glauca'']</ref><ref>Nuttall, Thomas. 1813. Catalogue of New and Interesting Plants Collected in Upper Louisiana no. 89.</ref>

==Distribution==
''Yucca glauca'' is native to central [[North America]]: occurring from the [[Canadian Prairie]]s of [[Alberta]] and [[Saskatchewan]] in [[Canada]]; south through the [[Great Plains]] to [[Texas]] and [[New Mexico]] in the [[United States]].<ref>{{cite web
|url = https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=YUGL
|title = Yucca glauca Nutt.
|work = Plants Profile
|publisher = [[United States Department of Agriculture]]
|access-date = 2012-09-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web

|publisher = [[University of Texas at Austin]]
|access-date = 2012-09-17}}</ref>

== Pollinators ==
The "honey ant" (''[[Myrmecocystus mexicanus]]''), among other species, has been observed collecting nectar from ''Y. glauca''.<ref>Conway, John R. "The Biology of Honey Ants."''The American Biology Teacher'', Vol. 48, No. 6 (Sep., 1986), pp. 335–343.</ref>

Yucca species are dependent on pollination by yucca moths, species in the genus ''[[Tegeticula]]'' and genus ''[[Parategeticula]]''. In turn the moths are dependent on yucca seeds as food for their larvae. This relationship was first scientifically observed by the botanist [[George Engelmann]] and entomologist [[Charles Valentine Riley]] in 1872 and has been the subject of many observations and experiments since then.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pellmyr |first1=Olle |title=Yuccas, Yucca Moths, and Coevolution: A Review |journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden |date=2003 |volume=90 |issue=1 |pages=35–55 |doi=10.2307/3298524 |jstor=3298524 |bibcode=2003AnMBG..90...35P |issn=0026-6493 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/10167 }}</ref>

When the bright white yucca flowers are in bloom, the female yucca moth visits a flower and collects a bundle of pollen.<ref name="USFS Pollinator">{{cite web |last1=Moisset |first1=Beatriz |title=Pollinator of the Month: Yucca Moths (''Tegeticula'' sp.) |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/pollinators/pollinator-of-the-month/yucca_moths.shtml |website=U.S. Forest Service |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240524010945/https://www.fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/pollinators/pollinator-of-the-month/yucca_moths.shtml |archive-date=24 May 2024 |language=en |url-status=live}}</ref> Though it is in the best interest of the plant that she then leaves to visit another plant, around two thirds of the time she visits a flower on the same inflorescence or even the same flower with the pollen collected when observed on ''[[Yucca filamentosa]]''.<ref name="Self Polination">{{cite journal |last1=Pellmyr |first1=Olle |last2=Massey |first2=Lisa K. |last3=Hamrick |first3=J. L. |last4=Feist |first4=Mary Ann |title=Genetic Consequences of Specialization: Yucca Moth Behavior and Self-Pollination in Yuccas |journal=Oecologia |date=1997 |volume=109 |issue=2 |pages=273–278 |doi=10.1007/s004420050083 |jstor=4221519 |pmid=28307179 |bibcode=1997Oecol.109..273P |language=en |issn=0029-8549}}</ref> Female yucca moths can smell if another moth has visited a bloom and prefer ones that have not been visited. This behavior is influenced by the plant because when moths lay too many eggs in a flower's ovary, the plant will abort the pod killing the moth's young.<ref name="USFS Pollinator" /> When a female lays eggs in the ovary of the flower, she then immediately climbs to the stigma and fertilizes the flower with pollen gathered previously to ensure food for her larvae.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pellmyr |first1=Olle |last2=Thompson |first2=John N. |last3=Brown |first3=Jonathan M. |last4=Harrison |first4=Richard G. |title=Evolution of Pollination and Mutualism in the Yucca Moth Lineage |journal=The American Naturalist |date=1996 |volume=148 |issue=5 |pages=827–847 |doi=10.1086/285958 |jstor=2463408 |bibcode=1996ANat..148..827P |language=en |issn=0003-0147}}</ref> If this exhausts her load of pollen she then goes to gather more before moving on again to investigate more flowers as potential sites to lay more eggs.<ref name="Self Polination" />

The specific species of yucca moth known to visit ''Yucca glauca'' flowers is ''[[Tegeticula yuccasella]]''. This species is also known to visit ''Yucca filamentosa''.<ref name="Self Polination" />

==Uses==
Soapweed yucca was a traditional Native American medical plant, used by the [[Blackfoot]], [[Cheyenne]], [[Lakota people|Lakota]], and other tribes.<ref name=NAE>{{cite web
|url = http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Yucca+glauca
|title = Native American Ethnobotany
|publisher = [[University of Michigan–Dearborn]]
|access-date = 2012-09-17}}</ref>

Among the [[Zuni people]], the seed pods are boiled and used for food.<ref>Stevenson, Matilda Coxe 1915 Ethnobotany of the Zuni Indians. SI-BAE Annual Report #30 p.73</ref> Leaves are made into brushes and used for decorating pottery, ceremonial masks, altars and other objects.<ref>Stevenson, p.82</ref> Leaves are also soaked in water to soften them and made into rope by knotting them together.<ref name="Stevenson, p.79">Stevenson, p.79</ref> Dried leaves are split, plaited and made into water-carrying head pads.<ref>Bell, Willis H and Edward F. Castetter 1941 Ethnobiological Studies in the Southwest VII. The Utilization of Yucca, Sotol and Beargrass by the Aborigines in the American Southwest. University of New Mexico Bulletin 5(5):1-74 (p. 47)</ref> Leaves are also used for making mats, cincture pads and other articles.<ref name="Stevenson, p.79"/> The peeled roots are pounded, made into suds and used for washing the head, wool garments and blankets.<ref>Stevenson, p.83</ref>

The young flower stalks and unripe fruits can be cooked and eaten.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=134|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref>

Yucca glauca is desirable as a landscaping plant, particularly for low water and high altitude gardens. It is an excellent choice for [[Xeriscaping]]. Not only do this hardy perennial's showy leaves make a striking display, but it is also cold hardy and drought tolerant. Its bell shaped flowers, typically cream colored, grow on tall spikes. This plant blooms in the summer. Yucca glauca is deer resistant. This plant can be propagated from seed that has been winterized, from root cuttings, and from stem cuttings. The tops of the leaves are needle sharp and must be handled with care. It is wise to plant them away from areas that are commonly traversed.<ref name=NCCE>{{cite web |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/yucca-glauca/ |title=Yucca glauca |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |publisher=North Carolina Cooperative Extension |access-date=25 February 2024}}</ref><ref name=GardenersHQ>{{cite web |url=https://www.gardenershq.com/Yucca-glauca.php |title=Small Soapweed Yucca (Yucca glauca) Growing & Care Guide for Gardeners |author=Dean Ravenscroft, Ph.D. |website=Gardeners HQ |date=1 February 2024 |publisher=Gardener's HQ |access-date=25 February 2024}}</ref>
